pos: n. (Nikolaus von Amsdorf, 1483–1565, Wittenberg theologian, bishop of Naumburg, leader of the Gnesio-Lutherans)
etymology: German Nikolaus, from Greek Nikolaos, victory of the people; von Amsdorf, of Amsdorf, a village of Thuringia.
biblical_def: Nikolaus von Amsdorf was the oldest of Luther's Wittenberg colleagues and the most immovable. He lectured at Wittenberg from 1511, stood beside Luther at the Leipzig disputation and at Worms, helped arrange the Wartburg hiding, and worked on the committee that revised the German Bible. In 1542 the elector installed him as bishop of Naumburg, and Luther consecrated him without any papal rite — the first evangelical bishop in Germany made by the church rather than by Rome. After Luther died, Amsdorf led the party that refused every imperial compromise, and when Melanchthon's circle conceded Roman ceremonies as indifferent things, Amsdorf answered that in a time of confession nothing is indifferent. His courage outran his precision at one point: pressing against Georg Major, he wrote that good works are detrimental to salvation. The Formula of Concord rejected that sentence as firmly as it rejected Major's, and it was right to. A man may be sound on the article of justification and still frame a sentence Scripture will not carry. Amsdorf's real service was that he would not let the doctrine be traded for peace: “Therefore, brethren, stand fast, and hold the traditions which ye have been taught” (2Th 2:15).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines detrimental as causing loss or damage, and adiaphorous as indifferent, neither good nor evil in itself.
webster_full: DETRIMENT'AL, a. Causing loss or damage; injurious; hurtful.
BISH'OP, n. An overseer; a spiritual superintendent or director.
CONSECRATE, v. To set apart and devote to the service of God.
INDIF'FERENT, a. Having no influence or preponderating weight; neither good nor evil.
scriptures: Eph 2:8
For by grace are ye saved through faith; and that not of yourselves: it is the gift of God:
Eph 2:9
Not of works, lest any man should boast.
Eph 2:10
For we are his workmanship, created in Christ Jesus unto good works, which God hath before ordained that we should walk in them.
Therefore, brethren, stand fast, and hold the traditions which ye have been taught, whether by word, or our epistle.
corruption_summary: The man who would not trade the article of justification for imperial peace, and who overshot in defending it.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The live misuse is the one Amsdorf himself fell into and the one he fought, which are opposite errors with a single root. He fought Major's sentence that good works are necessary to salvation, because it smuggles the worker back into the ground of his acceptance. He then wrote that good works are detrimental to salvation, which denies what the same apostle says in the next breath after denying works any part in justifying.

The principle to recover is that Scripture states both halves without embarrassment and refuses to let either swallow the other. “For by grace are ye saved through faith; and that not of yourselves: it is the gift of God” (Eph 2:8), and immediately, “For we are his workmanship, created in Christ Jesus unto good works, which God hath before ordained that we should walk in them” (Eph 2:10). Works are excluded from the foundation and required in the building. A theology that cannot hold both verses in one hand will keep producing an Amsdorf and a Major in every generation.

pos: n. (Georg Rörer, 1492–1557, Luther's amanuensis and the editor of his works)
etymology: German Georg, from Greek Georgios, a husbandman; Rörer, from Middle High German rörer, a reed-cutter.
biblical_def: Georg Rörer is the reason a great deal of Luther survives. He came to Wittenberg in 1522, was in 1525 the first man ordained by the evangelical rite there, and spent the rest of his life at a desk with a pen. He took down Luther's sermons and lectures in a shorthand of his own, sat on the committee that revised the German Bible through its successive printings, corrected the press, kept the manuscripts, and after Luther's death carried his papers to Jena when the Wittenberg succession turned. The Wittenberg edition of Luther's works is largely his labour. He is the kind of man a movement cannot do without and almost never names: no original doctrine, no famous confession, no martyrdom, only forty years of accurate transcription done at the speed of another man's speech. Scripture has a name for the office. Baruch sat under Jeremiah with ink and a roll, and when the king burned the roll, Baruch wrote it again. “He pronounced all these words unto me with his mouth, and I wrote them with ink in the book” (Jer 36:18).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines amanuensis as one who writes what another dictates, and transcribe as to copy, to write over again.
webster_full: AMANUEN'SIS, n. A person whose employment is to write what another dictates.
TRANSCRI'BE, v. To copy; to write over again or in the same words.
SHORT'HAND, n. A compendious method of writing by substituting characters for words.
EDI'TION, n. The publication of any book; also, the whole number of copies published at once.
scriptures: Then Baruch answered them, He pronounced all these words unto me with his mouth, and I wrote them with ink in the book.

Then took Jeremiah another roll, and gave it to Baruch the scribe, the son of Neriah; who wrote therein from the mouth of Jeremiah all the words of the book which Jehoiakim king of Judah had burned in the fire: and there were added besides unto them many like words.
Hab 2:2
And the LORD answered me, and said, Write the vision, and make it plain upon tables, that he may run that readeth it.
Luk 1:3
It seemed good to me also, having had perfect understanding of all things from the very first, to write unto thee in order, most excellent Theophilus,
corruption_summary: Luther's shorthand man, who wrote down what the Reformation said and kept the paper.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The live misuse is a habit of mind rather than a doctrine: the assumption that a movement is its famous names, so that the recording, copying, correcting and keeping are clerical work beneath notice. Rörer's career is the standing refutation. Remove him and a large part of Luther's preaching simply does not exist, because nobody else was writing it down.

The principle to recover is that God has always put the word in writing through men who were not the prophet. Baruch's name is in the text beside Jeremiah's, and the reason is plain: “Write the vision, and make it plain upon tables, that he may run that readeth it” (Hab 2:2). The vision is given to one man and made plain by another, and both offices are in the verse. Luke calls his own work writing “in order” (Luk 1:3), which is the same labour under a different name.

pos: n. (Johann Forster, 1496–1558, Hebraist of Wittenberg and lexicographer)
etymology: German Johann, from Hebrew Yochanan, the LORD is gracious; Forster, a forester, keeper of a wood.
biblical_def: Johann Forster taught Hebrew at Wittenberg and gave the Reformation one of its most useful and least celebrated tools. He studied under Reuchlin, joined Luther's Bible revision committee, and spent the better part of thirty years on a Hebrew dictionary built on a principle that was itself a confession: the sense of a Hebrew word is to be gathered from the way Scripture uses it, not received from the rabbinic commentators as a fixed gloss. His Dictionarium Hebraicum Novum appeared in 1557, the year before he died. Whatever its lapses — and a first attempt of that size has many — the method was sound and it was the method the whole Protestant translating enterprise would adopt. A man who makes a dictionary is doing for others what Ezra's Levites did for the assembly at the water gate: putting the text within reach of a people who cannot read it in the original. “So they read in the book in the law of God distinctly, and gave the sense, and caused them to understand the reading” (Neh 8:8).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines lexicon as a dictionary or word-book, and Hebraist as one versed in the Hebrew language.
webster_full: LEX'ICON, n. A dictionary; a vocabulary or book containing an alphabetical arrangement of the words in a language, with the definition of each.
HE'BRAIST, n. One versed in the Hebrew language.
RAD'ICAL, a. In philology, pertaining to the root; original; underived.
IN'TERPRET, v. To explain the meaning of words to a person who does not understand them.
scriptures: Neh 8:8
So they read in the book in the law of God distinctly, and gave the sense, and caused them to understand the reading.
Study to shew thyself approved unto God, a workman that needeth not to be ashamed, rightly dividing the word of truth.
The entrance of thy words giveth light; it giveth understanding unto the simple.
Act 8:30
And Philip ran thither to him, and heard him read the prophet Esaias, and said, Understandest thou what thou readest?
corruption_summary: The Wittenberg Hebraist who built a dictionary out of Scripture's own usage.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The live misuse is the modern habit of treating lexical work as neutral apparatus, as though a dictionary carried no commitments. Forster's did, and he said so. To define a Hebrew word by the range of its scriptural occurrences rather than by an inherited rabbinic gloss is to confess that Scripture interprets Scripture, and that the believing church reads the Old Testament in the light of the whole canon rather than under a borrowed authority.

The principle to recover is that a word-book is a servant of the pulpit and the plough, not an ornament of the academy. The point of the labour is the man in Acts who was reading aloud and could not follow what he read, and the question Philip put to him: “Understandest thou what thou readest?” (Act 8:30). The Levites at the water gate “gave the sense, and caused them to understand the reading” (Neh 8:8). A lexicon exists for that sentence or it exists for nothing.

pos: n. (Johannes Aurifaber, 1519–1575, Luther's last amanuensis and editor of the Table Talk)
etymology: Latin aurifaber, a goldsmith, a latinised form of the German surname Goldschmidt.
biblical_def: Johannes Aurifaber came late into Luther's household and was there at the end. He served as the old man's famulus in the last years, travelled with him to Eisleben in the winter of 1546, and stood in the room when he died. What he did afterwards fixed Luther in the memory of Germany more than any treatise did. Aurifaber gathered the notebooks of the men who had sat at Luther's table — his own, Lauterbach's, Cordatus's, others — and published the Tischreden in 1566, the book in which Luther talks rather than argues. He also edited the Jena edition of the works and brought out the letters. Scholars have grumbled ever since that he smoothed and arranged and sometimes improved his master's German, and the complaint is fair. It is also beside the main point: without him the table talk is a drawer of loose paper. He understood that words spoken in a house are worth the ink, and said so in the only way that counts, by buying the paper. “The preacher sought to find out acceptable words: and that which was written was upright, even words of truth” (Ecc 12:10).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines compilation as the act of collecting from various authors into one work, and memoir as an account of transactions familiarly written.
webster_full: COMPILA'TION, n. A collection of certain parts of a book or books into a separate book or pamphlet.
MEM'OIR, n. An account of transactions or events written in a familiar manner.
AMANUEN'SIS, n. A person whose employment is to write what another dictates.
COLLOQUY, n. Conversation; mutual discourse of two or more.
scriptures: The preacher sought to find out acceptable words: and that which was written was upright, even words of truth.
And further, by these, my son, be admonished: of making many books there is no end; and much study is a weariness of the flesh.
A word fitly spoken is like apples of gold in pictures of silver.
Precious in the sight of the LORD is the death of his saints.
corruption_summary: The man who published Luther's table talk and stood in the room at Eisleben.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The live misuse belongs to the Tischreden rather than to its editor. Because the book is Luther off duty — genial, coarse, overstated, contradicting himself across years — it is quarried for sentences to hang on him that he never argued in print and would not have defended. A remark made over supper and written down by a guest is evidence of a man's temper, not a standard of his doctrine.

The principle to recover is that the words a man weighs and the words a man drops are both his, and only one of them is his testimony. Solomon distinguishes the two by the labour: “The preacher sought to find out acceptable words: and that which was written was upright, even words of truth” (Ecc 12:10). Sought out, found, weighed, written. “A word fitly spoken is like apples of gold in pictures of silver” (Pro 25:11) — fitly, which is a judgment about the setting, not only the metal.

pos: n. (Georg Major, 1502–1574, Wittenberg theologian, named in the Majoristic controversy)
etymology: German Georg, from Greek Georgios, a husbandman; Major, Latin for greater, a latinised surname.
biblical_def: Georg Major was a Wittenberg professor and dean, a preacher of some weight, and the man whose name was fastened to a controversy he spent the rest of his life trying to get out from under. Pressed in the years after Luther's death to say what place works hold in the Christian life, he wrote that good works are necessary to salvation. He meant that no one is saved who goes on without them, which is what the New Testament says of a living faith. But the sentence as it stands puts works into the clause where salvation is decided, and Amsdorf and the Gnesio-Lutherans fell on it. Major qualified, retracted the formula, said he had never meant works as a cause, and finally asked that the phrase be dropped altogether. The Formula of Concord dropped it, and rejected Amsdorf's counter-sentence with it. The episode is a lesson in the cost of an imprecise clause in a public confession: “Hold fast the form of sound words, which thou hast heard of me” (2Ti 1:13).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines necessary as that must be, indispensably requisite, and controversy as a dispute or debate in words or writings.
webster_full: NEC'ESSARY, a. That must be; that cannot be otherwise; indispensably requisite.
CONTROVERSY, n. Dispute; debate; agitation of contrary opinions.
RETRACT', v. To recall, as a declaration or saying; to disavow; to recant.
FORM'ULA, n. A prescribed form; a rule or model.
scriptures: Rom 3:28
Therefore we conclude that a man is justified by faith without the deeds of the law.
Eph 2:10
For we are his workmanship, created in Christ Jesus unto good works, which God hath before ordained that we should walk in them.
Jam 2:17
Even so faith, if it hath not works, is dead, being alone.
Hold fast the form of sound words, which thou hast heard of me, in faith and love which is in Christ Jesus.
corruption_summary: The man whose careless clause cost the German churches twenty years.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The live misuse is the modern impatience with doctrinal precision, which hears the Majoristic controversy as theologians quarrelling over a preposition while the church burned. The preposition was the whole matter. Everything depends on whether works stand in the ground of a man's acceptance or in the fruit of it, and a confession that leaves the question open will be read both ways within a generation.

The principle to recover is that Scripture itself keeps the clauses separate and we are not free to blend them. “Therefore we conclude that a man is justified by faith without the deeds of the law” (Rom 3:28) settles the ground. “Even so faith, if it hath not works, is dead, being alone” (Jam 2:17) settles the evidence. Major wanted to say the second and said it in words that sounded like a denial of the first, which is why Paul's charge to Timothy is about the form of sound words and not merely their substance: “Hold fast the form of sound words” (2Ti 1:13).

pos: n. (Johann Mathesius, 1504–1565, pastor of Joachimsthal and Luther's first biographer)
etymology: German Johann, from Hebrew Yochanan, the LORD is gracious; Mathesius, a latinised form of Mathes, from Hebrew Mattithyahu, gift of the LORD.
biblical_def: Johann Mathesius read Luther's treatise on good works as a young schoolmaster, sold what he had, and went to Wittenberg. He boarded in Luther's house, took his turn at the table notebooks, and then went back to Joachimsthal in the Bohemian mountains, a silver-mining town, where he was rector and then pastor until he died. He is remembered for two bodies of preaching, and both are remarkable because of where they were delivered. The Sarepta sermons take the trades of his congregation — the shaft, the ore, the smelting, the assay — and preach the gospel through them to men whose working lives were underground. The other series is the first life of Luther, seventeen sermons preached to the same miners in 1562 and 1563, which is the source of a great deal that is known about Luther's early years. A country pastor in a mining valley wrote the biography and the industrial sermons both, which says something about where the Reformation actually took root. “And I will give you pastors according to mine heart, which shall feed you with knowledge and understanding” (Jer 3:15).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines ore as the compound of a metal and some other substance, and assay as the trial of the purity of metals.
webster_full: ORE, n. The compound of a metal and some other substance, as oxygen or sulphur, called its mineralizer.
ASSA'Y, n. The trial of the goodness, purity, weight and value of metals.
SMELT, v. To melt or fuse, as ore, for the purpose of separating the metal.
BIOG'RAPHY, n. The history of the life and character of a particular person.

corruption_summary: The mining-town pastor who preached the gospel through the shaft and wrote the first life of Luther.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The live misuse is the assumption that serious theology happens in capitals and universities, and that a parish in a mountain valley is where a man goes when he has nothing further to contribute. Mathesius had Wittenberg and chose Joachimsthal, and the two works that outlived him were both preached there to men with ore dust on them.

The principle to recover is that the promise of a fed people is not a promise of famous men. “And I will give you pastors according to mine heart, which shall feed you with knowledge and understanding” (Jer 3:15) is a promise about diet, not reputation. Peter puts the same office in the imperative and attaches it to a place: “Feed the flock of God which is among you” (1Pe 5:2) — among you, the particular people in the particular valley, which is the whole of a pastor's geography.

pos: n. (Erasmus Alber, c. 1500–1553, Lutheran hymnwriter, fabulist and controversialist)
etymology: Greek erasmios, beloved, desired; German Alber, from Old High German adalbero, noble bear.
biblical_def: Erasmus Alber studied under Luther at Wittenberg and then spent his life moving from post to post — schoolmaster, pastor, army chaplain, finally superintendent at Neubrandenburg, where he died within a year of arriving. He was a difficult man and his career shows it. What he left is better than his temper. He wrote some two dozen hymns that went into the German books and stayed there, plain verse meant to be sung by people who could not read music. He wrote a book of rhymed fables in the manner of Aesop with the moral turned toward the gospel, which did for the German nursery something of what the catechism did for the schoolroom. And he wrote a savage little book against the Franciscan Book of Conformities, the compilation that paralleled the life of Francis with the life of Christ; Luther wrote the preface. The fables and the hymns are the part that lasted, and both rest on a conviction about how truth travels into a household. “Let the word of Christ dwell in you richly in all wisdom; teaching and admonishing one another in psalms and hymns and spiritual songs” (Col 3:16).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines fable as a feigned story intended to enforce some useful truth, and hymn as a song of praise to God.
webster_full: FA'BLE, n. A feigned story or tale, intended to instruct or amuse; a fictitious narration intended to enforce some useful truth or precept.
HYMN, n. A song or ode in honour of God; among pagans, a poem in praise of a deity.
SU'PERINTENDENT, n. One who has the oversight and charge of something, with the power of direction.
CONFORM'ITY, n. Correspondence with a model or example; resemblance; agreement.

corruption_summary: Hymns for the people, fables for the children, and one furious book against a false parallel.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The live misuse is the one Alber attacked, in a newer dress. The Book of Conformities set the life of a saint alongside the life of Christ point for point, until the reader could not tell which figure the devotion was aimed at. The modern form rarely names a medieval friar; it runs the parallel with a founder, a movement, or a cause, and the effect is identical — the Lord becomes the pattern illustrating the man rather than the man a debtor to the Lord.

The principle to recover is the test Isaiah gives, which is a test of measurement and not of sincerity: “To the law and to the testimony: if they speak not according to this word, it is because there is no light in them” (Isa 8:20). Alber's constructive answer was better than his polemic. He put the word of Christ into verse a family could sing, which is exactly the apostolic instruction: “teaching and admonishing one another in psalms and hymns and spiritual songs” (Col 3:16).

pos: n. (Anton Lauterbach, 1502–1569, deacon of Wittenberg and diarist of Luther's table talk)
etymology: Latin Antonius, a Roman family name; German Lauterbach, clear brook, from lauter, pure, and Bach, a brook.
biblical_def: Anton Lauterbach was deacon at Wittenberg and afterwards superintendent at Pirna, and he kept the best of the table notebooks. Of all the men who sat in Luther's house with a pen, Lauterbach was the most methodical: he dated his entries, kept them in order through 1538 and the years around it, and recorded what was said rather than what would read well. When Aurifaber later assembled the published Tischreden he leaned heavily on Lauterbach's diary, and where the printed book and the diary disagree the historians take the diary. That is the whole measure of the man — a hundred and thirty years of Luther scholarship has treated his notebook as the control. He was besides a sound parish minister through the Interim years, holding a Saxon town steady while the imperial settlement pressed. Luke states the standard for the work Lauterbach did without knowing he was doing it: “having had perfect understanding of all things from the very first, to write unto thee in order” (Luk 1:3).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines diary as an account of daily events, and authentic as having a genuine original, of approved authority.

corruption_summary: The dated notebook that scholarship still uses to check the printed Table Talk.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The live misuse is the preference for the readable account over the accurate one, which is not a modern invention but has modern tools. Aurifaber's printed Tischreden is the better book to read; Lauterbach's diary is the better record of what was said. When the two part company, the smoother text is the one that moved.

The principle to recover is that certainty is the point of careful writing, and Luke says so outright. He wrote in order, and gave the reason for it: “That thou mightest know the certainty of those things, wherein thou hast been instructed” (Luk 1:4). A dated entry made the same evening is worth more than a polished recollection made twenty years on, and the church has always known it — which is why Baruch's account of his own method is in the canon: “I wrote them with ink in the book” (Jer 36:18).

pos: n. (the Leipzig Interim, 1548, the Saxon settlement with the imperial religious order)
etymology: German Leipzig, the Saxon city; Latin interim, in the meantime, a provisional arrangement.
biblical_def: The Leipzig Interim was the arrangement by which electoral Saxony tried to survive the emperor's victory without surrendering the gospel, and it nearly cost the German churches their confession. Charles V, having beaten the Schmalkaldic League, imposed the Augsburg Interim in 1548: Roman rites, Roman bishops, Roman ceremonies, with married clergy and the cup to the laity grudgingly allowed until a council should settle matters. Melanchthon and the Wittenberg theologians, under pressure from the new elector, drafted a Saxon version that conceded the ceremonies while holding the article of justification. Their defence was that rites are adiaphora, things indifferent, and may be yielded to keep the pulpits open. Flacius and the Magdeburg men answered that a ceremony surrendered under compulsion is no longer indifferent, because the surrender itself preaches. The controversy ran for thirty years, and the Formula of Concord decided it in Magdeburg's favour. The principle it settled is worth more than the vestments ever were: “Watch ye, stand fast in the faith, quit you like men, be strong” (1Co 16:13).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines interim as the meantime, the intervening time, and adiaphorous as indifferent, neither good nor evil.
webster_full: IN'TERIM, n. The meantime; the intervening time; the time between acts or events.
ADIAPH'OROUS, a. Indifferent; neutral; a word applied to things which are neither good nor evil in themselves.
CON'CESSION, n. The act of granting or yielding; the thing yielded.
CER'EMONY, n. Outward rite; external form in religion.
scriptures: Watch ye, stand fast in the faith, quit you like men, be strong.
Eph 6:13
Wherefore take unto you the whole armour of God, that ye may be able to withstand in the evil day, and having done all, to stand.
Therefore, brethren, stand fast, and hold the traditions which ye have been taught, whether by word, or our epistle.
Gal 1:8

corruption_summary: Saxony's attempt to keep the gospel by surrendering the ceremonies, and the thirty-year quarrel it caused.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The live misuse is the argument the Interim was built on and which is made afresh in every pressed generation: that a practice carrying no doctrine in itself may always be yielded, since only the doctrine matters. The Magdeburg answer stands. A thing indifferent in ordinary times stops being indifferent the moment an enemy demands it as the token of submission, because then it is no longer the rite that is being conceded but the right of the church to order her own worship.

The principle to recover is that standing is itself commanded and is not reducible to holding correct opinions quietly. “Watch ye, stand fast in the faith, quit you like men, be strong” (1Co 16:13) is four imperatives, and none of them is about what a man thinks. Paul adds the circumstance that makes the difference: “that ye may be able to withstand in the evil day, and having done all, to stand” (Eph 6:13). The evil day is precisely when the indifferent thing stops being indifferent.

pos: n. pl. (the Philippists, the party of Melanchthon's followers in the German churches, c. 1550–1580)
etymology: From Philipp Melanchthon, Greek Philippos, lover of horses; with the suffix -ist, a follower or adherent.
biblical_def: The Philippists were the men who held Wittenberg after Luther died and took their name from Philipp Melanchthon, whose learning, caution and horror of conflict they inherited together. They were not a sect and never meant to be a party; they were the university establishment, and the label was fastened on them by opponents. Three things divided them from the Gnesio-Lutherans: they defended the Leipzig Interim's concession of ceremonies, they spoke of the will as somehow cooperating in conversion, and on the Lord's Supper they moved steadily toward a position their enemies called Crypto-Calvinism — Christ truly received by faith rather than bodily present in the elements. In 1574 the elector of Saxony, convinced he had been deceived about how far the Wittenberg men had gone, arrested their leaders and broke the party; the Formula of Concord in 1577 wrote the Gnesio-Lutheran settlement into the confession. The irony is not small: on the Supper the Philippists were nearer the truth than the men who defeated them, and they lost anyway, because a party that will not say plainly what it believes cannot be defended when the test comes. “Hold fast the form of sound words” (2Ti 1:13).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines crypto as a prefix denoting concealment, and party as a number of persons united in opinion, in opposition to others.
webster_full: PAR'TY, n. A number of persons united in opinion or design, in opposition to others in the community.
CRYP'TICAL, a. Hidden; secret; occult.
DISSIM'ULATION, n. The act of dissembling; a hiding under a false appearance.
SCHISM, n. In a general sense, division or separation; a division or separation in a church.
scriptures: Now I beseech you, brethren, by the name of our Lord Jesus Christ, that ye all speak the same thing, and that there be no divisions among you; but that ye be perfectly joined together in the same mind and in the same judgment.
Hold fast the form of sound words, which thou hast heard of me, in faith and love which is in Christ Jesus.

Isa 8:20
To the law and to the testimony: if they speak not according to this word, it is because there is no light in them.
corruption_summary: Melanchthon's heirs, broken in 1574 for holding quietly what they would not confess plainly.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The live misuse is the strategy the Philippists adopted and which is still recommended as prudence: hold the better view, teach it by implication, avoid the word that would force a decision, and wait for the climate to change. It does not work, and the reason is not tactical. A conviction that is never stated is never defended, and when the elector finally asked the Wittenberg men directly what they believed about the Supper, the years of careful ambiguity counted against them rather than for them.

The principle to recover is that the apostolic call to unity is a call to say the same thing out loud, not to leave the disputed thing unsaid. “that ye all speak the same thing” (1Co 1:10) is a demand for a common confession, and the measure of it is public: “To the law and to the testimony” (Isa 8:20). Paul's charge to Timothy is about a form of sound words precisely because a form can be held out where a private persuasion cannot.
